project.name: node-mapnik-1
project.description: node-mapnik-1: a Greenstand fork of node-mapnik. Upstream C++/JS Node-API bindings to the Mapnik rendering toolkit, extended with a PostGIS-backed Express tile server (under greenstand/) that renders Tree Tracker web-map tiles. Note: this is a fork; the src/ layer documents upstream code.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to learn what node-mapnik is. This repository is a Greenstand fork of the upstream node-mapnik project, which binds the C++ Mapnik map-rendering toolkit to Node.js. The README covers installation, dependencies, and usage of the native bindings, giving you the base layer that the Greenstand tile server later builds on. Read it as context, then the rest of the tour focuses on the Greenstand-specific value under greenstand/.

tour.title: Tile Server Entry Point
tour.description: greenstand/app.js is the heart of the fork: an Express application that turns a tile request into a rendered PNG. For each z/x/y tile it builds a Mapnik map instance, injects a SQL query that reads from PostGIS, and streams back the image. This file is the root of the dependency graph for the whole tile server, so everything in the next steps hangs off it.
tour.languageLesson: Express route handlers are plain (req, res) callbacks. Rendering is asynchronous, so the handler builds the map, then uses a Mapnik render callback (or Promise) before calling res.send with the PNG buffer.

tour.title: Configuration and Projection
tour.description: app.js has two direct dependencies worth seeing early. config.js builds the Mapnik XML style configuration from templates, injecting the database connection string and the zoom-dependent SQL that decides between clustered and individual tree points. sphericalmercator.js converts the incoming tile x/y/z coordinates into a geographic bounding-box envelope, which is the spatial filter every tile query needs.

tour.title: Map Controller
tour.description: Building on the entry point from Step 2, Map.js is the request orchestrator. It inspects the request settings (tree id, user, wallet, timeline, zoom target) and selects the correct SQL query-builder class for that case, then runs the query against the PostGIS connection pool. This is the central routing logic that maps a tile request to the right data query.

tour.title: Database Connection Pooling
tour.description: PGPool.js wraps a PostgreSQL connection pool with an LRU cache and per-query request coalescing, so duplicate concurrent tile reads collapse into a single database hit. This matters because a web map fires many overlapping tile requests at once. Map.js from Step 4 runs its selected query through this pool.
tour.languageLesson: Request coalescing keys in-flight Promises by query. Concurrent callers await the same pending Promise instead of issuing duplicate queries, a common Node.js pattern for deduplicating async work.

tour.title: SQL Query Builders
tour.description: The classes under greenstand/sqls/ are the query-builders that Map.js chooses between. SQLCase1.js is the base builder for the user/wallet point query, assembling WITH, JOIN, filter, and bounding-box clauses for tree captures at a given zoom. Its Timeline and zoom-target variants specialize the same shape for different views, while SQLTree.js fetches a single tree joined with species, planter, token, and wallet data.

tour.title: Mapnik Style and XML Injection
tour.description: Once the SQL is chosen, it must be handed to Mapnik. XMLConfig.js holds an embedded Mapnik XML map template and exposes a class that injects the SQL query into the PostGIS datasource parameter, while xml.js exports the reusable style template strings. This is the seam where a database query becomes a renderable map definition.

tour.title: Mapnik Stylesheets and Data
tour.description: These non-code assets define how features look on the tile. postgis.xml is the Mapnik layer that renders active trees from a PostGIS datasource as point symbols with a text label style, and stylesheet.xml is the full web-mercator stylesheet with polygon, line, and point symbolizers plus a GeoJSON tree layer. trees.json supplies sample point features. Together they are the visual contract the rendered PNG obeys.
tour.languageLesson: Mapnik XML defines Layers bound to a datasource plus Styles made of Rules and Symbolizers. A PostGIS datasource takes a table parameter that can be a full sub-select, which is exactly what XMLConfig.js injects.

tour.title: Native Mapnik Bindings
tour.description: Underneath the tile server sits the upstream native rendering layer. lib/mapnik.js loads the compiled Mapnik binary and augments it with JS helpers, and lib/index.js is the barrel that re-exports it, which is what app.js requires. On the C++ side, node_mapnik.cpp is the addon entry point that registers all bindings, mapnik_map.hpp declares the Map wrapper the server instantiates, and mapnik_vector_tile.hpp declares the vector-tile API. Treat this as the engine the Greenstand server drives, not something you edit.

tour.title: Packaging and Containerization
tour.description: package.json defines the server dependencies, scripts, and the native build wiring, and the Dockerfile packages everything into a runnable image. The Dockerfile starts from the dadiorchen/tile2 base, installs C++ tooling and Node.js 14, compiles the native Mapnik bindings via make release_base, and launches the app with npm start. This is how the code from Steps 2-9 becomes a deployable container.
tour.languageLesson: This Dockerfile is single-stage: it keeps build tooling in the final image. Native Node addons must be compiled against the same Node ABI they run on, which is why the build happens inside the image rather than being copied in.

tour.title: Kubernetes Deployment
tour.description: The tile server runs on Kubernetes via Kustomize. deployment/base/deployment.yaml declares the pod and container built from Step 10, service.yaml exposes it inside the cluster, and kustomization.yaml ties the base together so environment overlays (development, production) can patch it. This shows how the container reaches production.
tour.languageLesson: Kustomize layers a base plus overlays: the base holds common manifests, and each overlay patches image tags, secrets, and mappings per environment without duplicating the whole spec.

tour.title: CI/CD Pipelines
tour.description: The capstone is automation. build-deploy.yml builds and deploys the image, while the deploy-dev, deploy-prod, and deploy-test workflows promote it across environments using the Kustomize overlays from Step 11. This closes the loop from a code change to a running tile server serving Greenstand Tree Tracker maps.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows trigger on push or dispatch events. Jobs run in parallel by default; steps within a job run sequentially, and one workflow can build an image while others handle per-environment deploys.
